decks.title: Natural Vegetation — Part 1: Forests, evergreen and deciduous
goals: Explain the ecological and economic importance of forests
Correlate the features of tropical evergreen and deciduous forests with rainfall and temperature
Name important trees of each type and their uses

slides.heading: From rainforest to thorn scrub
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **natural vegetation** is the plant cover that grows on its own, without being planted by people. In India it changes mainly with **rainfall**, and in the mountains with **altitude**.

visual.alt: Table of the main vegetation types of India with rough rainfall and an example area

slides.narration: Namaste! Natural vegetation means the plants that grow on their own, without being planted. India has dense rainforests, monsoon forests that drop their leaves, thorny scrub in the desert, mangroves on muddy coasts and changing belts of trees on the mountains. Mostly, it is the amount of rain that decides which kind grows where. In this part we study why forests matter and the two great tropical forest types.

slides.heading: Ecological importance of forests
slides.body_md: **Forests protect the environment:** trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen; they **moderate temperature** and add moisture to the air through transpiration, helping rainfall; **roots bind the soil** and leaf litter slows runoff, so forests **check soil erosion and floods**; rainwater soaks in slowly, **recharging groundwater** and keeping streams flowing after the rains; they provide **habitat** for wildlife and conserve biodiversity; leaf litter adds **humus** to the soil.

nodes.label: Roots bind soil; litter slows water

visual.alt: Flow showing how forest cover slows water, reduces erosion and floods, and keeps streams flowing

slides.narration: Forests look after the environment. Trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and the water they release into the air helps cool it and bring rain. Their roots hold the soil, and fallen leaves slow the flow of rainwater, so less soil is washed away and floods are smaller. Water soaks into the ground and feeds springs long after the rains. Forests are also home to countless animals and plants.

slides.heading: Economic importance of forests
slides.body_md: **Forests support livelihoods and industry:** **timber** for buildings, furniture, railway sleepers and boats; **fuelwood** and **fodder** for villages; **raw materials** for paper (bamboo, softwood), plywood, matches, rayon and sports goods; **minor forest products** — lac, gum, resin, honey, cane, tendu leaves (for bidis), medicinal plants such as cinchona (quinine); food and income for **tribal communities**; and **tourism** in national parks.

visual.alt: Table of forest products and their uses

slides.narration: Forests also feed the economy. They give timber for houses, furniture and railway sleepers, firewood and fodder for villages, and raw materials for paper, plywood and match factories. They give lac, gum, honey, cane and medicinal plants, and the leaves used to wrap bidis. For many tribal families the forest is their store, their pharmacy and their source of income.

slides.heading: Quick check: why forests matter
slides.body_md: Tell an ecological benefit from an economic one.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ecological benefits protect soil, water, air and wildlife; economic benefits are products and income.

slides.heading: Rainfall decides the forest type
slides.body_md: In the tropical lowlands of India, **annual rainfall** is the main control: over about **200 cm** — tropical evergreen; **100–200 cm** — moist deciduous; **70–100 cm** — dry deciduous; **under 70 cm** — thorn forest and scrub. Temperature matters too: these forests need warmth all year, which is why altitude changes the picture in the mountains.

slides.narration: Look at this rainfall scale. Where more than about two hundred centimetres of rain falls each year, we find tropical evergreen forest. Between one hundred and two hundred centimetres, moist deciduous forest grows. From seventy to one hundred, dry deciduous forest. Below seventy, only thorny trees and bushes survive. Each illustrative station sits in the band that matches its rainfall.

slides.heading: Tropical evergreen forests
slides.body_md: **Climate:** rainfall over 200 cm, high temperature (about 25–27 °C) and humidity all year. **Distribution:** western slopes of the **Western Ghats**, hills of the **north-east** (Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal), the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**. **Characteristics:** very **dense**, with several **storeys**; tall trees (often 40–60 m); trees shed leaves at different times, so the forest is **green all year**; many species grow **mixed together**; climbers and undergrowth. **Trees:** ebony, mahogany, rosewood, rubber, cinchona, with bamboo and canes. **Hardwoods** are valuable but hard to extract.

slides.narration: Tropical evergreen forests grow where it is hot and wet all year, with more than two hundred centimetres of rain. They cover the western slopes of the Western Ghats, the north eastern hills and the Andaman Islands. They are so dense that sunlight barely reaches the ground, and the trees grow in several storeys. There is no fixed season of leaf fall, so the forest stays green. Ebony, mahogany and rosewood grow here.

slides.heading: Worked example: rich forest, little timber
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The evergreen forests of the north-east contain valuable hardwoods, yet they supply far less commercial timber than the deciduous forests of Madhya Pradesh. Give reasons.

**Step 1. Mixed stands.** Many species grow together, so a logger finds only a few trees of any one kind in an area.

**Step 2. Density and terrain.** Thick undergrowth, climbers and hilly ground make felling and hauling difficult and costly.

**Step 3. Transport.** Remote areas have few roads, and the hardwood logs are very heavy.

**Step 4. Climate.** Heavy rain for much of the year limits the working season.

nodes.label: Dense growth, hilly land, few roads

visual.alt: Flow showing why mixed, dense, remote evergreen forests yield little commercial timber

slides.narration: Why do these rich forests give so little timber to industry? Many kinds of trees grow mixed together, so there are few trees of any one kind in one place. The forest is thick with climbers and bushes, often on steep hills with few roads, and hardwood logs are very heavy. Heavy rain also shortens the season when work is possible. So logging is slow and expensive.

slides.heading: Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests
slides.body_md: The most widespread forests of India, also called **monsoon forests**. Trees **shed their leaves for six to eight weeks** in the dry summer to **reduce water loss**. **Moist deciduous** (100–200 cm): the north-eastern states along the Himalayan foothills, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, eastern slopes of the Western Ghats — **teak, sal, shisham, sandalwood, bamboo, khair, arjun**. **Dry deciduous** (70–100 cm): drier parts of the peninsular plateau and the plains of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh — open stands of **teak, sal, peepal, neem**; grassy patches. Fairly **pure stands** of one species make them **commercially the most important** forests.

rows: Chota Nagpur, Odisha, foothills, eastern Ghats slopes
Plateau interior, Bihar and UP plains

visual.alt: Table comparing moist and dry deciduous forests

slides.narration: Tropical deciduous forests are the most widespread in India and are often called monsoon forests. In the dry hot season their trees drop their leaves for some weeks to save water. Moist deciduous forests grow where rain is between one hundred and two hundred centimetres, with teak, sal and sandalwood. Dry deciduous forests grow in drier areas and are more open, with teak, peepal and neem.

slides.heading: Important trees and their uses
slides.body_md: Learn trees **with their uses**: **teak** — strong, durable timber for furniture, doors and boats; **sal** — hard timber for railway sleepers and building; **sandalwood** (Karnataka) — carving, perfume oil, incense; **shisham** — furniture; **bamboo** — paper pulp, building, baskets; **khair** — katha; **ebony** — fine furniture and carving; **mahogany** and **rosewood** — high-quality furniture; **cinchona** — quinine; **rubber** — latex.

visual.alt: Table of important trees with their forest type and use

slides.narration: In the exam, name a tree together with its use. Teak gives strong timber for furniture and boats. Sal gives hard timber for railway sleepers. Sandalwood from Karnataka is carved and used for perfume oil. Ebony, mahogany and rosewood make fine furniture. Cinchona bark gives quinine, a medicine for malaria, and bamboo is pulped to make paper.

slides.heading: Worked example: matching stations to forests
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Four illustrative stations have these annual rainfall totals. Name the natural vegetation of each and one typical tree.

**P** (windward slope of the Western Ghats, 280 cm) → tropical evergreen

**Q** (Chota Nagpur plateau, 140 cm) → moist deciduous

**R** (plains of south Bihar, 85 cm) → dry deciduous

**S** (western Rajasthan, 30 cm) → tropical desert (thorn)

**Trees.** P: ebony or rosewood; Q: sal or teak; R: teak, peepal or neem; S: babul or khejri.

**Method.** Compare each total with the band limits (200, 100 and 70 cm).

visual.alt: Table of four illustrative stations with rainfall and expected vegetation

slides.narration: To classify a station, compare its rainfall with the band limits. Station P, on the windward Western Ghats, gets far more than two hundred centimetres, so it has evergreen forest. Station Q, on the Chota Nagpur plateau, falls between one and two hundred, so moist deciduous. Station R gets between seventy and one hundred, so dry deciduous. Station S, in the desert, has thorn forest.

slides.narration: Quick check. Deciduous trees drop their leaves in the dry season to save water.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Forests: ecological value (soil, water, climate, oxygen, wildlife) and economic value (timber, fuel, fodder, industry, minor products, tribal livelihoods).
Tropical evergreen: over 200 cm, hot and humid; dense, storeyed, green all year; ebony, mahogany, rosewood; hard to exploit.
Tropical deciduous: monsoon forests; shed leaves in the dry season; moist (100–200 cm) and dry (70–100 cm); teak, sal, sandalwood; most important commercially.

visual.alt: Summary table of forest types with rainfall and a key tree

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Forests protect soil, water and climate, and give timber, fuel, fodder and many other products. Tropical evergreen forests grow in the wettest areas; they are dense and green all year but hard to log. Tropical deciduous forests, the monsoon forests, drop their leaves in the dry season and give valuable teak and sal.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: "Correlate with climate": link each feature to rain or temperature (dense because of heavy rain; leaf fall because of a dry season).
Give distribution with named regions, not just "the south".
Separate ecological and economic importance clearly.

rows: Deciduous forests are hard to log
They are the main source of timber

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. When asked to correlate a forest with climate, link each feature to the rain or temperature that causes it. Name regions when you give distribution. Always add a use when you name a tree. And keep ecological benefits, which protect nature, separate from economic benefits, which are products and income.

goals: Explain how desert plants and mangroves are adapted to their environment

slides.heading: Plants at the edges
slides.body_md: Part 2 — some of India’s plants live in very harsh places: dry sand, salty tidal mud and cold mountain slopes. Each has special features that help it survive. We also see how India is trying to protect and extend its forests.

visual.alt: Table of harsh conditions, the vegetation found there and an example place

slides.narration: Some plants live in very harsh conditions. In the desert there is little water, on muddy coasts the water is salty and the tide comes and goes, and on high mountains it is cold. Each kind of vegetation has special features that help it survive. In this part we look at desert, tidal and mountain vegetation, and then at how we can protect and grow our forests.

slides.heading: Tropical desert (thorn) vegetation
slides.body_md: **Climate:** rainfall under about 70 cm, long dry season, hot summers. **Distribution:** western Rajasthan, Kutch and Saurashtra in Gujarat, south-west Punjab and Haryana, dry parts of the Deccan in the rain-shadow. **Adaptations:** **long roots** that reach deep water; **small, thorny or waxy leaves** that lose little water; **thick, fleshy stems** that store water (cacti, euphorbias); trees widely scattered. **Plants:** babul (acacia), khejri, kikar, ber, wild palms, cacti, euphorbias. **Uses:** fuel, fodder, gum from babul, tanning bark.

visual.alt: Table of desert plant adaptations and how each helps

slides.narration: In the desert there is very little rain and a long dry season. Plants such as babul, khejri and cacti survive by saving water. Their roots run very deep to reach water underground. Their leaves are small, thorny or waxy, so they lose little water. Some have thick fleshy stems that store water. The trees grow far apart, each one drawing water from a wide area.

slides.heading: Littoral or tidal forests: mangroves
slides.body_md: **Where:** on muddy coasts and **deltas** washed by tides — the **Ganga–Brahmaputra delta (Sundarbans)**, the deltas of the **Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri**, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. **Adaptations:** they tolerate **salty water**; **stilt (prop) roots** hold them in soft mud; **breathing roots (pneumatophores)** grow upward and take in air at low tide, because waterlogged mud lacks oxygen. **Trees:** **sundari** (hard, durable timber for boats), keora, agar, nipa palm. **Value:** protect coasts from storm waves and erosion; fish breeding grounds; habitat of the Bengal tiger in the Sundarbans.

slides.narration: Mangroves are the forests of muddy, salty coasts and deltas, such as the Sundarbans. The tide floods them twice a day. The sundari tree gives hard, lasting timber for boats. Mangroves also shield the coast from storm waves.

slides.heading: Mountain vegetation: zones with altitude
slides.body_md: In the Himalayas, **temperature falls with altitude** (about 6.5 °C per 1000 m), so vegetation changes in belts, much as it would travelling towards the poles. Approximate zones: **foothills** — tropical moist deciduous (sal); **about 1000–2000 m** — wet temperate forest of **oak and chestnut**; **about 2000–3000 m** — **coniferous** forest of **pine, deodar, spruce, silver fir, cedar**; **about 3000–3600 m** — alpine forest of silver fir, juniper, birch, rhododendron; **above about 3600 m** — **alpine meadows**, used for summer grazing by herders such as the Gujjars and Bakarwals; higher still, mosses and lichens, then snow.

slides.narration: As you climb a mountain it gets colder, so the plants change in belts. In the Himalayan foothills sal forests grow. Higher up come forests of oak and chestnut, then cone bearing trees such as pine, deodar, spruce and fir. Near the tree line there are junipers, birches and rhododendrons. Above that are alpine meadows where herders graze their flocks in summer, and finally only mosses and lichens below the snow.

slides.heading: Worked example: temperature and altitude
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** At the foot of a Himalayan range (illustrative) the mean summer temperature is 30 °C. Taking a fall of 6.5 °C per 1000 m, estimate the temperature at 2000 m and at 3000 m, and say which forest you would expect at each.

**Step 1.** At 2000 m: $30 - 6.5 \times 2 = 17$ °C → cool: the boundary between oak–chestnut and coniferous forest.

**Step 2.** At 3000 m: $30 - 6.5 \times 3 = 10.5$ °C → cold: the upper limit of coniferous forest, giving way to alpine trees.

**Step 3. Conclusion.** Falling temperature, not rainfall, explains the belts of mountain vegetation.

visual.alt: Table of illustrative temperatures at three altitudes with the vegetation expected

slides.narration: Suppose it is thirty degrees at the foot of a range and the air cools by six and a half degrees for every thousand metres. At two thousand metres it would be about seventeen degrees, cool enough for oak and conifers. At three thousand metres it would be about ten and a half degrees, near the upper limit of the conifers. So it is falling temperature that makes the belts.

slides.heading: Why forests must be conserved
slides.body_md: Forests are lost to **clearing for farms, roads, dams, mines and towns**, **overgrazing**, **fuelwood cutting**, **forest fires** and **shifting cultivation**. Loss of forest brings **soil erosion, floods and droughts**, **silting of reservoirs**, loss of **wildlife**, and hardship for people who depend on forests. **Forest conservation** means protecting existing forests and **increasing tree cover** through planned planting and careful use.

visual.alt: Flow showing causes of forest loss and its effects

slides.narration: Forests are cleared for farms, roads, dams, mines and towns. Too many animals graze, people cut wood for fuel, and fires spread. When forests disappear, soil is washed away, floods and droughts grow worse, reservoirs fill with silt, wildlife loses its home and forest people lose their living. Conservation means protecting the forests we have and adding new tree cover.

slides.heading: Methods: afforestation, reforestation, social forestry, agroforestry
slides.body_md: **Afforestation:** planting trees on land that has **not had forest** (or not for a very long time), such as wasteland and dunes. **Reforestation:** **replanting** trees where a forest has been **cut or burnt**. **Social forestry:** planting trees on **public and community land** — roadsides, canal banks, railway land, village commons — to meet local needs for **fuel, fodder and small timber**, with people’s participation. **Agroforestry:** growing **trees together with crops** (and sometimes livestock) on the **same farmland**, giving extra income and protecting the soil. **Van Mahotsav:** a **tree-planting festival** started in **1950**, held every year in the **first week of July** to make people aware of the value of trees and to plant saplings.

rows: Land where forest was cut or burnt

visual.alt: Table comparing afforestation, reforestation, social forestry, agroforestry and Van Mahotsav

slides.narration: Afforestation means planting trees where there was no forest, such as on wasteland. Reforestation means replanting where a forest has been cut or burnt. Social forestry plants trees on public land, like roadsides and canal banks, to give villagers fuel and fodder. Agroforestry grows trees and crops together on a farm. And Van Mahotsav is a tree planting festival held every July since nineteen fifty.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming the method
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the method in each case and give a reason.

**(a)** Saplings are planted on sand dunes near Bikaner that have never carried forest. → **Afforestation:** new forest on land without one.

**(b)** A sal forest burnt in Jharkhand is replanted. → **Reforestation:** an old forest is restored.

**(c)** A panchayat in Haryana plants neem and shisham along canal banks for villagers’ fuel and fodder. → **Social forestry:** public land, community benefit.

**(d)** A Punjab farmer grows poplar between rows of wheat. → **Agroforestry:** trees and crops on the same farm.

slides.narration: To name the method, ask a few questions. Was there a forest before? If not, planting is afforestation. If the forest was cut or burnt and is being replanted, it is reforestation. If trees are planted on public land to meet the needs of villagers, it is social forestry. And if a farmer grows trees among his crops, it is agroforestry.

notes.title: Natural Vegetation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Importance of forests
sections.body_md:
- **Natural vegetation:** plant cover that grows without being planted by people.
- **Ecological:** oxygen and carbon dioxide balance; moderate temperature and add moisture (help rainfall); roots bind soil, litter slows runoff (less erosion, smaller floods); groundwater recharge; habitat and biodiversity; humus.
- **Economic:** timber, fuelwood, fodder; raw material for paper, plywood, matches, rayon; minor products (lac, gum, resin, honey, cane, tendu leaves, medicinal plants); tribal livelihoods; tourism.

key_terms.definition_md: Plant cover that grows on its own, without human planting.
Forest products other than timber, such as lac, gum, honey, cane and tendu leaves.

visual.alt: Table contrasting ecological and economic importance of forests

sections.heading: 2. Tropical evergreen forests
sections.body_md:
- **Climate:** over 200 cm rain; hot and humid all year.
- **Distribution:** western slopes of the Western Ghats; north-eastern hills; Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
- **Features:** very dense; several storeys; tall trees; leaves shed at different times (green all year); many species mixed; climbers and undergrowth.
- **Trees:** ebony, mahogany, rosewood, rubber, cinchona; bamboo and canes.
- **Exploitation is difficult:** mixed stands, dense growth, hilly remote land, heavy logs.

key_terms.definition_md: Never bare of leaves as a whole, because trees shed leaves at different times.

visual.alt: Table linking evergreen forest features to causes

sections.heading: 3. Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests
sections.body_md:
- **Leaf fall:** trees shed leaves for 6–8 weeks in the dry summer to reduce water loss.
- **Moist deciduous (100–200 cm):** north-east along the foothills, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, eastern slopes of the Western Ghats; teak, sal, shisham, sandalwood, bamboo, khair, arjun.
- **Dry deciduous (70–100 cm):** drier plateau, plains of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh; teak, sal, peepal, neem; open with grass.
- **Most important commercially:** large area, valuable timber, fairly pure stands, easier access.

| Tree | Use |
|---|---|
| Teak | Furniture, doors, boats |
| Sal | Railway sleepers, building |
| Sandalwood | Carving, perfume oil |
| Bamboo | Paper pulp, building |

key_terms.definition_md: Another name for tropical deciduous forests, which shed their leaves in the dry season.

sections.heading: 4. Tropical desert and littoral vegetation
sections.body_md:
- **Desert (thorn):** under 70 cm; western Rajasthan, Kutch, Saurashtra, south-west Punjab and Haryana; long roots, small thorny or waxy leaves, fleshy stems; babul, khejri, kikar, ber, cacti, euphorbias.
- **Littoral (tidal) or mangrove:** deltas of the Ganga–Brahmaputra (Sundarbans), Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri; Andaman and Nicobar; salt-tolerant; **stilt roots** for support; **breathing roots (pneumatophores)** for air; sundari (boat timber), keora, agar, nipa.
- Mangroves protect coasts from storm waves, trap silt and shelter fish and wildlife.

sections.heading: 5. Mountain vegetation
sections.body_md:
- Temperature falls with altitude (about 6.5 °C per 1000 m), so vegetation changes in belts.
- **Foothills:** tropical moist deciduous (sal).
- **About 1000–2000 m:** wet temperate — oak, chestnut.
- **About 2000–3000 m:** temperate coniferous — pine, deodar, spruce, silver fir, cedar.
- **About 3000–3600 m:** alpine — silver fir, juniper, birch, rhododendron.
- **Above about 3600 m:** alpine meadows (summer grazing); mosses and lichens; then snow.
- Altitudes are approximate and vary from east to west.

key_terms.definition_md: Cone-bearing trees with needle-shaped leaves, such as pine and deodar.
High grasslands above the tree line, used for summer grazing.

sections.heading: 6. Forest conservation
sections.body_md:
- **Threats:** clearing for farms, roads, dams, mines and towns; overgrazing; fuelwood; fires; shifting cultivation.
- **Afforestation:** trees on land without forest (wasteland, dunes).
- **Reforestation:** replanting where forest was cut or burnt.
- **Social forestry:** trees on public and community land (roadsides, canal banks, village commons) for local fuel, fodder and small timber.
- **Agroforestry:** trees grown with crops on the same farmland.
- **Van Mahotsav:** tree-planting festival started in 1950, held every year in the first week of July; aim — awareness of the value of trees and planting saplings.

**Assertion (A):** Forests help to recharge groundwater.

**Reason (R):** Roots and a layer of fallen leaves let rainwater soak slowly into the ground instead of running off.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: Give two ways in which the forests of the Nilgiri hills help to conserve soil and water for the plains below.

answer.model_answer_md: Tree roots bind the soil on the slopes and fallen leaves cover the ground, so heavy rain washes away less soil. The forest floor slows runoff and lets rain soak in, recharging groundwater and keeping the streams that flow to the plains running after the rains.

questions.solution_md: Soil held by roots and litter; water soaks in, streams flow longer.

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which the forests of the Bastar region are important to the tribal people who live there.

answer.model_answer_md: They provide food, fuelwood, fodder and building material for daily needs. They also give income from minor products such as tendu leaves, lac, honey, gum and medicinal plants that the people collect and sell.

questions.solution_md: Daily needs; income from minor products.

questions.stem_md: A hill district in Uttarakhand loses most of its forest cover. Explain three effects this is likely to have on the district and the plains downstream.

answer.model_answer_md: Without roots and leaf litter, rain washes the topsoil off the slopes, so farmland loses fertility and landslides increase. Runoff reaches the rivers quickly, so floods downstream become sudden and severe, while springs dry up after the rains because less water soaks in. The eroded soil settles as silt in rivers and reservoirs, and wildlife and forest-based livelihoods are lost.

questions.solution_md: Erosion; floods and drying springs; silting and loss of livelihoods.

options.text_md: reduce the loss of water through their leaves

questions.solution_md: Leaf fall cuts transpiration during the dry season — option (b).

questions.solution_md: 70–100 cm with open stands → dry deciduous — option (a).

questions.solution_md: 140 cm lies between 100 and 200 cm → moist deciduous — option (c).

questions.solution_md: Option (a).

questions.solution_md: Option (b).

questions.stem_md: Tropical deciduous forests are commercially the most important forests of India because:

options.text_md: they are found only on the Andaman Islands
they consist mostly of softwood conifers
they cover a large area and yield valuable timber such as teak and sal in fairly pure stands

questions.solution_md: Option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Tropical evergreen forests have several storeys of trees.

**Reason (R):** Heavy rain and high temperatures throughout the year allow plants to grow all the time and compete for sunlight.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains the layered structure — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Tropical deciduous forests are also called monsoon forests.

**Reason (R):** They grow in regions that have no dry season.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false: these forests have a marked dry season, when the trees shed their leaves — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A lowland station receiving only 40 cm of rain a year would naturally support tropical evergreen forest.
questions.solution_md: False: under about 70 cm supports only thorn forest and scrub.

questions.stem_md: Tropical deciduous forests are also called ___ forests.
questions.solution_md: **Monsoon** forests.

questions.stem_md: Quinine, a medicine for malaria, is obtained from the bark of the ___ tree of the evergreen forests.
questions.solution_md: **Cinchona**.

questions.stem_md: Name one tree of the tropical moist deciduous forests that yields valuable timber.
questions.solution_md: Teak.

questions.stem_md: Relate two features of the forests on the windward slopes of the Western Ghats to the climate of the region.

answer.model_answer_md: Heavy rain (over 200 cm) and high temperatures all year let plants grow continuously, so the forest is very dense with several storeys of tall trees. As there is no long dry season, trees shed leaves at different times and the forest stays green all year.

questions.solution_md: Dense and storeyed (rain, warmth); evergreen (no dry season).

questions.stem_md: A forest in Chhattisgarh gets about 150 cm of rain a year and one on the plains of south Bihar about 80 cm. Name the forest type of each and one tree found in each.

answer.model_answer_md: Chhattisgarh: tropical moist deciduous forest, with sal (or teak, bamboo). South Bihar: tropical dry deciduous forest, with neem (or peepal, teak).

questions.solution_md: Moist deciduous with sal; dry deciduous with neem.

questions.stem_md: Compare tropical evergreen and tropical deciduous forests under three heads: rainfall, leaf shedding and commercial value.

answer.model_answer_md: Rainfall: evergreen forests need over about 200 cm; deciduous forests grow with about 70–200 cm. Leaf shedding: evergreen trees shed leaves at different times, so the forest is never bare; deciduous trees shed their leaves together in the dry season. Commercial value: evergreen forests are hard to exploit because species are mixed and access is poor; deciduous forests, with fairly pure stands of teak and sal, are the main source of timber.

questions.solution_md: Rainfall; leaf shedding; commercial value.

questions.stem_md: Plants such as babul and cactus in western Rajasthan have small or thorny leaves mainly to:

options.text_md: reduce the loss of water by transpiration

questions.solution_md: Small leaves lose less water — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A khejri tree near Barmer stays green through months without rain. The most likely reason is that:

options.text_md: it receives rain in every month of the year
its large broad leaves trap dew
its long roots reach water deep below the surface

questions.solution_md: Deep roots tap groundwater — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Mangrove trees of the Sundarbans have roots that grow upward out of the mud. These breathing roots help the trees to:

options.text_md: store water for the dry season
take in air, because the waterlogged mud has little oxygen
climb other trees to reach sunlight

questions.solution_md: Pneumatophores take in air at low tide — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Timber of the sundari tree of the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta is valued for boat-building mainly because it is:

options.text_md: hard and durable, even in water
soft and easy to bend into baskets

questions.stem_md: Littoral (tidal) forests are found mainly in:

options.text_md: the deltas of the Ganga, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri

questions.stem_md: After a cyclone, villages behind a thick belt of mangroves on the Odisha coast suffered less damage than open stretches of coast nearby. The best explanation is that mangroves:

options.text_md: stop cyclones from forming over the sea
break the force of storm waves and hold the coastal mud in place
raise the land far above sea level

questions.solution_md: Dense roots and trunks act as a natural barrier — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Climbing from the foothills towards the snowline in Himachal Pradesh, a trekker passes sal forest, then oak and chestnut, then pine and deodar, and finally meadows. The main reason for this change is that:

options.text_md: the soil becomes more fertile with height
the land becomes flatter with height

questions.solution_md: Cooling with height produces belts of vegetation — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Deodar, pine, spruce and fir are typical of which belt of Himalayan vegetation?

options.text_md: Tropical moist deciduous forest of the foothills
Temperate coniferous forest, roughly 2000 to 3000 m

questions.solution_md: Option (c).

questions.stem_md: In summer, Gujjar and Bakarwal herders take their flocks up to:

options.text_md: alpine meadows high in the Himalayas
the mangrove swamps of the Sundarbans
the evergreen forests of the Andamans

questions.solution_md: High pastures above the tree line are used for summer grazing — option (a).

**Assertion (A):** Vegetation in the Himalayas changes from tropical to alpine types as one climbs.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.stem_md: Match each approximate altitude in the Himalayas (Column A) with its typical vegetation (Column B).
questions.solution_md: Foothills → sal; 1000–2000 m → oak, chestnut; 2000–3000 m → pine, deodar; above 3600 m → meadows.

questions.stem_md: Match each forest type in Column A with a tree typical of it in Column B.
questions.solution_md: Evergreen → ebony; moist deciduous → teak; thorn → babul; littoral → sundari.

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which trees such as babul and khejri near Barmer are able to survive the dry climate.

answer.model_answer_md: Their roots grow very long and spread wide, so they can reach water deep underground. Their leaves are small, thorny or waxy, so they lose very little water through transpiration (some desert plants also store water in fleshy stems).

questions.solution_md: Long roots; small, thorny or waxy leaves.

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which mangrove trees of the Sundarbans survive in salty, tidal mud.

answer.model_answer_md: They tolerate salt water that would kill most plants, and their stilt roots anchor them firmly in the soft mud against the tides. Breathing roots grow upward out of the mud and take in air at low tide, since the waterlogged mud has little oxygen.

questions.solution_md: Salt tolerance and stilt roots; breathing roots.

questions.stem_md: Describe how vegetation changes with altitude in the Himalayas, naming one tree in each of three belts.

answer.model_answer_md: Temperature falls with height, so vegetation changes in belts. In the foothills below about 1000 m, tropical moist deciduous forest with sal grows. From about 1000 to 2000 m there is wet temperate forest of oak and chestnut; from about 2000 to 3000 m, coniferous forest of pine, deodar and fir. Higher up come alpine trees such as birch and juniper, then alpine meadows, mosses and lichens.

questions.solution_md: Belts with altitude, one tree each.

questions.solution_md: New forest on land without one — option (c).

questions.solution_md: An existing forest is restored — option (a).

questions.solution_md: Public land, community benefit — option (c).

questions.solution_md: Trees and crops on the same farm — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Van Mahotsav, started in 1950, is:

options.text_md: a movement in which villagers hugged trees
a law that bans all tree felling
a tree-planting festival held every year in July
a national park in the Himalayas

questions.solution_md: Option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Agroforestry can give farmers extra income.

**Reason (R):** Van Mahotsav is celebrated in the first week of July.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the date of Van Mahotsav does not explain why agroforestry adds income (timber, fruit and fodder from the trees do) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Reforestation means planting trees on land that has never carried a forest.
questions.solution_md: False: that is afforestation; reforestation is replanting where forest was cut or destroyed.

questions.stem_md: The tree-planting festival held in India every year in the first week of July is called ___.
questions.solution_md: **Van Mahotsav**.

questions.stem_md: State the aim of Van Mahotsav.

answer.model_answer_md: To make people aware of the value of trees and encourage them to plant and care for saplings.

questions.solution_md: Awareness and tree planting.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between afforestation and reforestation.

answer.model_answer_md: Afforestation is planting trees on land that has not carried forest, such as wasteland or dunes, to create a new forest. Reforestation is replanting trees on land where a forest has been cut, burnt or otherwise destroyed, to restore it.

questions.solution_md: New forest versus restored forest.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between social forestry and agroforestry, giving an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Social forestry is planting trees on public and community land, such as roadsides, canal banks and village commons, to meet local needs for fuel and fodder; for example, trees along canal banks in Haryana. Agroforestry is growing trees together with crops on private farmland; for example, poplar among wheat fields in Punjab.

questions.solution_md: Public land versus farmland, with examples.

questions.stem_md: A treeless village on the plains of Haryana needs fuelwood and fodder and wants to protect its fields from hot summer winds. Suggest three forest-conservation measures from this chapter, with a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Social forestry: plant fast-growing trees on roadsides, canal banks and the village common land to supply fuelwood and fodder without cutting other forests. Agroforestry: farmers grow trees such as poplar or shisham on field boundaries, which also gives extra income and acts as a windbreak against hot winds. Celebrate Van Mahotsav each July with school and village planting drives, so that people care for the saplings.

questions.solution_md: Social forestry; agroforestry; Van Mahotsav (afforestation of wasteland also accepted).

questions.stem_md: At the foot of a Himalayan range (illustrative) the mean summer temperature is 30 °C. If temperature falls by 6.5 °C for every 1000 m, what is the expected temperature at 2000 m, in °C?
questions.solution_md: Temperature $= 30 - 6.5 \times 2 = 17$ °C.

questions.stem_md: Using the same illustrative figures (30 °C at the foot of the range, a fall of 6.5 °C per 1000 m), find the expected temperature, in °C, at 3600 m, near the upper limit of trees.
questions.solution_md: Fall $= 6.5 \times 3.6 = 23.4$ °C; temperature $= 30 - 23.4 = 6.6$ °C.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state has the following forest areas in sq km (illustrative): moist deciduous 6000, dry deciduous 3600, tropical evergreen 1800, mangrove (littoral) 600. What percentage of its forest is moist deciduous?

Using the same illustrative forest areas (moist deciduous 6000, dry deciduous 3600, tropical evergreen 1800, mangrove (littoral) 600 sq km), find the share of tropical evergreen forest as a percentage of the total.

(a) State two ecological benefits of forests. [2]

(b) State two economic benefits of forests, naming a forest product for each. [2]

(c) Correlate three features of tropical evergreen forests with the climate in which they grow. [3]

(d) Name three trees of tropical evergreen forests and state one use of each. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) They check soil erosion and floods, as roots bind soil and litter slows runoff; they recharge groundwater and moderate the climate (also give oxygen and shelter wildlife).

(b) Timber for furniture and building (teak, rosewood); raw material for industry, such as bamboo for paper (also minor products like lac, honey and tendu leaves).

(c) Heavy rain over 200 cm and high temperature all year → very dense forest with several storeys of tall trees; no marked dry season → leaves shed at different times, so the forest is evergreen; constant warmth and moisture → many species grow mixed together, with climbers and undergrowth.

(d) Ebony — fine furniture and carving; mahogany or rosewood — high-quality furniture; cinchona — quinine for malaria (rubber — latex).

questions.solution_md: Ecological; economic; features with climate; trees with uses.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Why are tropical deciduous forests also called monsoon forests? [2]

(b) An imagined state has these forest areas in sq km (illustrative): moist deciduous 6000, dry deciduous 3600, tropical evergreen 1800, mangrove (littoral) 600. Calculate the share of moist deciduous and of dry deciduous forest in its total forest area. [2]

(c) Give three reasons why tropical deciduous forests are commercially the most important forests of India. [3]

(d) Name three trees of tropical deciduous forests and state one use of each. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) They grow in regions of monsoon climate with a distinct dry season, and their trees shed leaves for some weeks in that dry season to save water.

(b) Total $= 12000$ sq km; moist deciduous $= \frac{6000}{12000} \times 100 = 50$%; dry deciduous $= \frac{3600}{12000} \times 100 = 30$%.

(c) They cover the largest area of any forest type; they yield valuable timber such as teak and sal; trees of one kind grow in fairly pure stands, and the forests are more accessible, so logging is easier and cheaper.

(d) Teak — furniture, doors and boats; sal — railway sleepers and building; sandalwood — carving and perfume oil (bamboo — paper pulp).

questions.solution_md: Monsoon climate; 50% and 30%; area, timber, pure stands; trees with uses.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name two regions of India where tropical desert vegetation is found. [2]

(b) Name two trees of littoral forests and state where such forests grow. [2]

(c) Explain three ways in which desert plants are adapted to a dry climate. [3]

(d) Explain why mangroves are important for the coastal people of the Sundarbans. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Western Rajasthan and Kutch in Gujarat (also south-west Punjab and Haryana).

(b) Sundari and keora (also agar, nipa); in the tidal deltas of the Ganga–Brahmaputra, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, and on the Andaman and Nicobar coasts.

(c) Long roots reach water deep below the surface; small, thorny or waxy leaves reduce water loss by transpiration; thick, fleshy stems store water for the dry months, and plants grow far apart.

(d) Mangroves break the force of storm waves and cyclones and stop the coast from being eroded; they provide timber for boats, fuelwood, honey and thatch; their roots shelter fish, crabs and prawns, on which many families depend.

questions.solution_md: Desert regions; littoral trees and areas; adaptations; value of mangroves.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Why does natural vegetation change with altitude in the Himalayas? [2]

(b) The mean summer temperature at the foot of a range is 30 °C (illustrative), and it falls by 6.5 °C for every 1000 m. Calculate the expected temperature at 1000 m and at 3000 m. [2]

(c) Describe the vegetation found between about 1000 m and 3000 m, naming two trees. [3]

(d) Explain how the alpine meadows and the coniferous forests of the Himalayas are useful to people. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Temperature falls with height (and conditions become colder and windier), so plants suited to warmth give way to those suited to cold, producing belts of vegetation.

(b) At 1000 m: $30 - 6.5 = 23.5$ °C; at 3000 m: $30 - 6.5 \times 3 = 10.5$ °C.

(c) From about 1000 to 2000 m: wet temperate forest of broad-leaved trees such as oak and chestnut. From about 2000 to 3000 m: temperate coniferous forest of tall, cone-shaped trees with needle leaves, such as pine, deodar, spruce and silver fir.

(d) Alpine meadows provide summer pasture for the flocks of herders such as the Gujjars and Bakarwals. Coniferous forests give softwood for construction, furniture and paper pulp, resin from pine for turpentine, and fuelwood; they also protect slopes from erosion.

questions.solution_md: Temperature falls; 23.5 °C and 10.5 °C; oak, chestnut, pine, deodar; pastures and softwood.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between afforestation and reforestation. [2]

(b) What is Van Mahotsav? When did it begin? [2]

(c) Explain social forestry and agroforestry, with an example of each. [3]

(d) Give three reasons why forest conservation is necessary in India. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Afforestation creates new forest by planting trees on land without forest, such as wasteland; reforestation restores forest by replanting where it has been cut or burnt.

(b) A national tree-planting festival held every year in the first week of July to spread awareness of the value of trees; it began in 1950.

(c) Social forestry is planting trees on public and community land, such as roadsides, canal banks and village commons, to meet local needs for fuel, fodder and small timber — for example, canal-bank planting in Haryana. Agroforestry is growing trees along with crops on farmland, giving extra income and protecting the soil — for example, poplar among wheat fields in Punjab.

(d) Forests are being lost to clearing, overgrazing and fires, which leads to soil erosion, floods and silting of reservoirs; many people depend on forests for fuel, fodder and income; forests are home to wildlife and help keep the climate and water cycle balanced.

questions.solution_md: Afforestation and reforestation; Van Mahotsav; social forestry and agroforestry; reasons.
